common_name: Roscoff Onion (Oignon Rosé de Roscoff, Brittany Pink Onion)

planting.note: Start seed under cover in late winter and transplant young onions into light, sandy coastal soil in early spring, as traditionally grown on the Léon coast of northern Brittany.

directions: This copper-pink, slightly flattened storage onion has been grown around Roscoff in northern Brittany since the 17th century and holds French AOC protection recognizing that regional history. Its flesh is dense and more pungent than sweet Mediterranean onion types, which combined with a tight, tissue-paper skin gives it unusually good keeping quality through winter. Grow it on light, well-drained soil close to the coast if possible, since local growers credit the sea air and sandy loam for the variety's distinctive bite and storage life. Cure bulbs fully in a dry, airy spot before braiding or storing, the traditional Breton method for hanging strings of onions through the winter months.
sources: INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité) AOC Oignon de Roscoff dossier
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity Ark of Taste
Kokopelli Seed Foundation

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or potted vines in early spring in well-drained, sunny ground, and train onto a sturdy trellis or traditional pergola to expose the dense fruit clusters to maximum light and airflow.

directions: Chasselas de Moissac was the first fruit variety in France to receive AOC protection, in 1971, recognizing its long cultivation around Moissac in the Tarn-et-Garonne valley. The vine produces loose clusters of thin-skinned, amber-green grapes with a crisp, sweet, almost musky flavor that is prized for eating fresh rather than for winemaking. It is notably cold-hardy for a table grape, which is part of why it has long been grown as far north as Switzerland and Alsace as well as in the warmer southwest of France. Thin developing clusters if they are overly dense to improve berry size and ripening, and harvest in early autumn once the grapes turn translucent amber.
sources: INAO AOC Chasselas de Moissac dossier
University of California Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology
French Ministry of Agriculture geographical indication records

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in early spring at soil level in raised, well-drained rows; Gariguette is an early, short-day type often grown under tunnels in southwest France to bring the harvest forward.

directions: Gariguette is France's most celebrated strawberry, bred in the 1970s and now closely associated with the Périgord and Lot-et-Garonne growing regions where it is typically the first fresh strawberry of the French market season. The elongated, bright orange-red berries are notably aromatic and sweet-tart with a firm bite, qualities that have made it the benchmark variety against which other French strawberries are judged. As a short-day type, it sets most of its flower buds in response to shortening autumn daylength, concentrating fruiting into one intense spring flush rather than the long trickle produced by day-neutral types. Mulch under the fruiting trusses to keep berries clean and remove runners during the growing season unless propagating new plants.
sources: INRAE (Institut National de Recherche pour l'Agriculture, l'Alimentation et l'Environnement) strawberry breeding records
Chambre d'Agriculture Nouvelle-Aquitaine fruit production guides
Cornell Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained loam; the cultivar is self-fertile, so a single tree can produce a full crop without a pollinizer.

directions: Prune d'Ente is the European plum cultivar behind the Pruneau d'Agen, France's famous dried prune, grown commercially across the Lot-et-Garonne valley in southwest France. The oval purple-skinned fruit has firm, sweet, low-moisture flesh and a freestone pit, traits that have long made it especially well suited to drying rather than fresh eating, though tree-ripened fruit is also enjoyed fresh. It is self-fertile and a reliable, consistent bearer once established, generally beginning to produce meaningful crops within three to four years of planting. Harvest when fruit is fully colored and slightly soft for drying, since under-ripe fruit dries poorly and loses much of the variety's characteristic rich, caramel-like sweetness.
sources: Bureau National Interprofessionnel du Pruneau (BNIP)
University of California Cooperative Extension Fruit & Nut Research Information Center
Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

planting.note: Plant certified disease-free rhizomes in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and provide a tall trellis of at least 14 to 18 feet, since this low-yielding aroma variety needs ample bine length to produce a worthwhile cone harvest.

directions: Strisselspalt is the signature aroma hop of Alsace, grown around the region's historic hop gardens near Strasbourg and long used in classic French and Belgian-style farmhouse ales and lagers. It is a low-alpha, high-aroma noble-type hop valued for delicate floral, spicy, and herbal notes rather than bitterness, so it is used primarily as a late or finishing addition in the brew kettle. Yields are modest compared with high-alpha American cultivars, and cones are small, which is typical of the European noble hop group it belongs to. Harvest when cones feel dry, papery, and springy to the touch, and dry promptly to preserve the delicate aromatic oils that define its character.
sources: Hop Growers of America
John I. Haas, Inc. hop variety catalog
Barth-Haas Group hop variety yearbook

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Tanche is largely self-fertile but sets a somewhat better crop with a compatible cultivar such as Aglandau nearby.

directions: Tanche is the cultivar behind Olives Noires de Nyons, France's first olive product to earn AOC protection, grown in the Drôme valley of the Rhône corridor around Nyons and Buis-les-Baronnies. It is notably cold-hardy for an olive, a trait that allows the orchards here to survive winters at the cooler northern edge of French olive country. The round, plump black fruit is traditionally left to fully ripen on the tree before being harvested and dry-salt cured, giving a wrinkled, meaty, mildly bitter table olive quite different from green-picked types. The same fruit also yields a mild, nutty, lightly almond-scented oil when a portion of the harvest is pressed rather than cured.
sources: AFIDOL (Association Française Interprofessionnelle de l'Olive)
INAO AOC Olives Noires de Nyons dossier
International Olive Council

planting.note: Plant in early spring in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; Grossane benefits from a nearby pollinizer such as Aglandau or Picholine to improve fruit set.

directions: Grossane is one of the principal cultivars behind the AOC olives of the Vallée des Baux-de-Provence, grown in the limestone hill country between Arles and Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It produces a notably large, plump, round fruit, as its name suggests, with tender flesh that is typically harvested green and cured for the table rather than pressed for oil. The tree has a moderately vigorous, spreading habit and crops reliably once mature, though like many Provençal olives it establishes slowly in its first several years after planting. Protect young trees from hard frosts and prune to keep the canopy open, since good light penetration improves both fruit size and consistent annual bearing.
sources: AFIDOL (Association Française Interprofessionnelle de l'Olive)
INAO AOC Olives Cassées de la Vallée des Baux-de-Provence dossier
International Olive Council

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil with wide spacing to support its very large, dense heads, the type long grown around Strasbourg for commercial sauerkraut production.

directions: Quintal d'Alsace is a historic late-season cabbage from the Alsace region of northeastern France, bred for the enormous, dense, flattened-round heads that once made it the mainstay of the region's choucroute industry. Heads can reach well beyond the size of typical storage cabbages, with crisp, thick, pale green leaves that shred well and hold their texture through fermentation. It is a long-season type best started early and given generous spacing and rich, moisture-retentive soil to support its heavy heads. Harvest in fall once heads are solid, and the variety also stores respectably in a cool root cellar if not fermented immediately.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation
Graines Baumaux
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity Ark of Taste
